notes: Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal appeal; dishonesty and strike-off reasoning is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Wells v Law Society: strike-off appeal dismissed for lateness and merits
key_facts: Steven Wells and Matthew Lamb, directors of Listers Solicitors in Bradford, admitted extensive breaches before a Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal.
Lamb was suspended for three years; Wells was found dishonest in relation to client fund misuse and the MML mortgage management scheme and struck off.
Wells' appeal notice was lodged over two years late after protracted public funding and solicitor changes.
The MML scheme held large client sums in a solicitors' client account while paying minimal interest and misleading vulnerable clients about Law Society protection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal under preserved RSC Order 106, with an application to extend time.
enrichment.outcome: Extension of time refused and appeal dismissed; strike-off upheld with costs order against Wells.
enrichment.ratio: Late appeals against strike-off require prompt and good explanation; where dishonesty is properly found on distinct evidence from a co-director who avoided such findings, differential sanctions including strike-off are justified and an appellate court will not interfere.
legal_issues: Whether time to appeal should be extended
Whether dishonesty findings against Wells were perverse or inconsistent with Lamb's suspension
Application of Royal Brunei and Twinsectra dishonesty test
Appropriateness of strike-off for dishonest misuse of client funds and MML conduct
linked_authorities: Royal Brunei Airlines Sdn Bhd v Tan [1995] 2 AC 378

confidence.notes: Findings, dishonesty test and final orders are clearly recorded.

notes: Unduly lenient sentence reference on long-running charity fraud; Pound increased to six years.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: Talbot Village Trust fraud sentences increased for architect Pound
key_facts: Guy Pound, Anthony Green and Peter Beard were convicted after a year-long trial of conspiracy to defraud the Talbot Village Trust over six building projects from 1985 to 1996.
Pound, the trust architect, dishonestly obtained about £1m in excessive fees and helped divert a further £1m to others including quantity surveyors and contractors.
Green and Beard received suspended nine-month sentences; Pound received three years' imprisonment.
Compensation and confiscation orders totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds were made against all three.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's references under section 36 of the 1988 Act following Crown Court sentencing.
enrichment.outcome: Pound's sentence quashed and substituted with six years' imprisonment; Green's and Beard's suspended sentences left undisturbed as acts of mercy.
enrichment.ratio: A gross long-term breach of professional trust warranting a substantially higher sentence may justify increasing an unduly lenient custodial term despite double jeopardy; where personal mitigation and prior confiscation orders make immediate imprisonment disproportionate, the court may decline to increase suspended sentences even if lenient on paper.
legal_issues: Whether section 36 references were in time where compensation and confiscation were adjourned
Construction of 'the last of the sentences' in Schedule 3
Appropriate sentence for dominant architect in eleven-year charity fraud
Application of double jeopardy on unduly lenient references

confidence.notes: Sentencing dispositions and jurisdictional reasoning are explicit.

notes: Cooksley guideline application; death by dangerous driving reference succeeds.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: death by dangerous driving sentence increased after red-light collision
key_facts: Stephen Chambers pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving and making off without payment after leaving a Coventry petrol station without paying.
He drove through a red light at a busy crossroads and pelican crossing, killing Mrs McPartland and injuring a lollipop lady and a child.
He failed to stop and continued to drive dangerously while trying to escape; he was uninsured, disqualified and seeking heroin.
The Crown Court imposed three and a half years' imprisonment with a seven-year disqualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 treating the leave application as the reference hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Reference granted; sentence increased from three and a half to four and a half years' imprisonment, allowing for double jeopardy.
enrichment.ratio: Driving through long-red traffic lights into a pelican crossing with visible pedestrians falls within the most serious Cooksley category with a not-guilty starting point of six years or more; numerous aggravating features justify a higher starting point, moderated only by early plea and limited remorse and by double jeopardy on reference.
legal_issues: Categorisation under R v Cooksley sentencing guidelines
Whether discrete aggravating features were double-counted
Appropriate increase on Attorney General's reference
Effect of double jeopardy on substituted sentence
linked_authorities: R v Cooksley and Others [2004] 1 Cr App R(S) 1

confidence.notes: Facts, guideline analysis and substituted sentence are clearly reasoned.

notes: Brief section 287 local plan challenge; dismissal and procedural limits are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Foster v Poole: section 287 local plan challenge dismissed as merits-based
key_facts: Mr Foster sought to challenge the Poole Local Plan First Revision under section 287 of the 1990 Act.
His objections concerned planning merits such as a new harbour bridge, housing on Canford Heath and loss of heathland.
He also made unsupported allegations of corruption, theft, intimidation and harassment unrelated to plan adoption procedures.
The application was unsupported by proper evidence and an adjournment for documents was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 287 challenge to adoption of a local development plan.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; objections held not arguable under section 287.
enrichment.ratio: Section 287 challenges are limited to unlawfulness or procedural failure causing substantial prejudice in adopting the plan, not a further opportunity to debate planning merits or unrelated misconduct; bare assertions without evidence cannot succeed.
legal_issues: Scope of section 287 grounds
Whether planning merit objections are justiciable on plan adoption
Appropriateness of adjournment
Proper forum for complaints about councillor conduct

confidence.notes: Short judgment but clear statement of section 287 limits and outcome.

notes: Leading PI damages appeal on Section 21 care and top-up awards; remittal in Sowden.

enrichment.short_title: Sowden and Crookdake: local authority care costs and top-up damages

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Two catastrophic brain injury claims raised whether future care and accommodation damages should be assessed on private provision or local authority Section 21 residential care.
Regulations disregard court-administered compensation so authorities cannot recover care costs from damages, potentially shifting burden from tortfeasors to councils.
In Sowden the judge preferred augmented residential care but top-up feasibility was insufficiently explored; in Crookdake the judge held statutory provision materially inadequate.
Defendants conceded substantial top-up sums if residential care was appropriate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals from High Court assessments of future care and accommodation damages.
enrichment.outcome: Sowden appeal allowed in part for limited remittal on practicability of top-up care; Crookdake appeal dismissed; 50% contributory negligence does not affect damages assessment method.
enrichment.ratio: Damages follow the compensatory principle comparing reasonable requirements with likely Section 21 provision; if augmented statutory care meets reasonable needs the tortfeasor need not fund private care, but top-up proposals must be particularised and evidentially tested and a judge may remit where late concessions prevented feasibility assessment.
legal_issues: Effect of Section 21 and assessment regulations on tort damages
Whether best interests or reasonable requirements is the correct test
Permissibility and evidential basis of top-up awards
Whether damages are assessed in the 100% world before contributory negligence reduction
linked_authorities: R v North and East Devon Health Authority ex parte Coughlan [2001] QB 213
Bell v Todd [2002] Lloyds Rep Med 12
Kelly v Stockport Corporation [1949] 1 All ER 893

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme, outcomes in both appeals and remittal order are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Patent licence jurisdiction and forum discretion; appeal dismissed with clear contract analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Celltech v MedImmune: English jurisdiction upheld for Synagis royalty dispute
key_facts: Celltech sued MedImmune for royalties under a 1998 patent licence covering Synagis sales where manufacture or sale would infringe a Valid Claim.
MedImmune commenced parallel US proceedings seeking declarations of invalidity and non-infringement of US Adair 2.
Clause 13.2 conferred English law and jurisdiction over disputes relating to validity, construction and performance of the agreement.
MedImmune applied to stay the English action in favour of the US forum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of stay and directions for streamlined trial in the Patents Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; English proceedings to continue with costs summarily assessed.
enrichment.ratio: A dispute whether royalties are payable because a product falls within a Valid Claim is a dispute about performance of the licence and within an English jurisdiction clause; strong reasons are needed to depart from contractual forum choice and parallel US validity proceedings do not outweigh the parties' bargain or risk of inconsistent construction given Celltech's undertaking on claim construction.
legal_issues: Construction of 'performance' in clause 13.2
Whether scope of foreign patent claims is justiciable in England via renvoi
Discretionary stay where contract selects English jurisdiction
Risk of inconsistent US validity and English scope decisions
linked_authorities: Donohue v Armco Inc [2002] 1 Lloyd's Rep 425
British Aerospace plc v Dee Howard Co [1993] 1 Lloyd's Rep 405

confidence.notes: Contract construction and discretionary reasoning are explicit though exclusive jurisdiction was not finally decided.

notes: TCC amendment/limitation ruling on fire spread claim; partial allowance with case management directions.

enrichment.short_title: Mersey Docks v Birse: limitation and amendment ruling after cold store fire
key_facts: A fire at a Hartlip cold storage centre in August 1997 caused losses of about £16.5 million against Birse and design subcontractors.
Claimants sought to amend particulars alleging additional fire compartment defects, failure to warn and failure to procure collateral warranties.
Defendants argued new causes of action were time-barred under the Limitation Act and CPR Part 17.4.
Many original documents were destroyed in the fire, complicating pleading.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application to amend particulars after end of limitation period.
enrichment.outcome: Several amendments allowed where new causes arose from substantially the same facts in the proceedings, subject to further case management and revised pleading process; discretion deferred on compromise terms.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 17.4(2) permits a new claim if it arises from the same or substantially the same facts as a claim for which the applicant already sought a remedy in the proceedings, not merely against the same defendant; whether a new cause of action exists requires comparison at a high level of abstraction of essential facts to be proved.
legal_issues: What constitutes a new cause of action under Letang v Cooper
Construction of CPR 17.4(2) 'in the proceedings'
Whether failure to procure collateral warranty is a new cause of action
Discretion to refuse amendments under the overriding objective
linked_authorities: Paragon Finance plc v Thakerar [1999] 1 All ER 400
Aldi Stores Ltd v Holmes Buildings plc [2003] EWCA Civ 1882

confidence.notes: Limitation analysis is detailed though final discretion on several amendments was deferred.

notes: Minimum term review applying Sullivan transitional guidance; term reduced to 15 years.

enrichment.short_title: R v Johnston: murder minimum term reduced under Sullivan guidance
key_facts: Johnston was convicted of murder after driving his car at a group in Aldershot following a failed heroin purchase.
Christopher Vickers, an innocent bystander, was killed when Johnston mounted the pavement and ran over him.
The trial judge specified an 18-year minimum term, treating use of the car as a weapon and absence of remorse as aggravating.
Sentencing proceeded on outdated December 2003 guidance rather than Sullivan transitional provisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against minimum term following Single Judge refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; minimum term reduced from 18 to 15 years less one year on remand.
enrichment.ratio: For murders committed between 31 May 2002 and 18 December 2003, Amendment No 8 to the Practice Direction applies with a normal 12-year starting point unless exceptionally high culpability features apply; use of a car as a weapon may aggravate but absence of remorse is not an aggravating factor, and mitigating lack of intent to kill and lack of premeditation must be weighed.
legal_issues: Application of R v Sullivan transitional minimum term guidance
Whether car used as weapon equates to explosives-type aggravation
Whether absence of remorse can aggravate minimum term
Proper balancing of aggravating and mitigating features

confidence.notes: Guideline correction and substituted term are clearly explained.

notes: WWTBAM copyright summary judgment applications; mixed outcomes across three claimants.

enrichment.short_title: Celador v Melville, Boone and Baccini: Millionaire format copyright applications
key_facts: Celador sought summary judgment on claims that Who Wants to Be a Millionaire copied formats submitted by three freelance creators.
WWM evolved from David Briggs' Cash Mountain proposals developed by Celador between 1995 and 1998.
Melville claimed Millionaires' Row was copied via TV companies including Carlton; Boone claimed HELP! was copied after submission to ITV.
Baccini claimed his Millionaire TV format and BT Lottery premium-line funding concept were copied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined CPR Part 24.2 summary judgment applications in copyright and breach of confidence claims.
enrichment.outcome: Melville and Baccini claims proceed to trial; Boone claim struck out as abuse of process and lacking real prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: Summary judgment requires no real prospect of success on copying; inference of copying may survive where similarities and timing raise a triable issue, but relitigation after an earlier related action may be abusive under Henderson v Henderson, and isolated stylistic similarities without a substantial part of the work cannot establish infringement.
legal_issues: CPR 24.2 real prospect test for copyright copying
Whether Revised Proposal existence and disclosure are triable issues
Abuse of process where Boone did not join earlier Watch TV proceedings
Whether similarities in TV formats constitute copying a substantial part
index_terms: Who Wants to Be a Millionaire
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1

notes: Case stated on section 5 sight requirement; appeal allowed on unusual facts.

enrichment.short_title: Holloway v DPP: section 5 requires conduct actually within someone's sight
key_facts: Alan Holloway filmed himself naked in woodland while focusing a video camera on schoolchildren playing sport on a nearby field.
No one actually saw him naked, though anyone could have done so; footage later showed him undressed with children in the background.
The magistrate convicted of section 5 disorderly/insulting behaviour likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress.
Holloway appealed by case stated on whether unseen but seeable conduct suffices.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Chester Magistrates' Court conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and conviction quashed; fine and costs remitted.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5 requires threatening, abusive or insulting behaviour to be within the actual sight or hearing of a person likely to be caused harassment, alarm or distress; it is not enough that someone might have seen the conduct, though the prosecution need not call a witness if the court can infer people were present who could see or hear.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'within the sight of a person' in section 5(1)
Contrast with section 3 affray and notional person of reasonable firmness
Whether inference of presence suffices without direct witness evidence
Distinction between could have been seen and could be seen

confidence.notes: Statutory construction issue and acquittal are clearly resolved on the stated facts.
